articles.title: Brentwood bookshop The Chicken and Frog to close due to bill rise
articles.summary: The Chicken and Frog in Brentwood says business rates and electricity bills have risen dramatically.
articles.body:
An independent bookshop described as being a "haven" for families and neurodivergent children has announced it will close after 14 years.

The Chicken and Frog says it will leave Brentwood town centre in January after a huge increase in its bills and business rates.

Owner Natasha Radford, aka "Mrs Chicken", also says the town's footfall has been so low that at times she has gone a whole day without a sale.

The 53-year-old said she had been busy since announcing the news, with customers coming in for a hug and a farewell.

"It means the world because running your own business is difficult. It becomes all-consuming," said Radford, a former teacher.

"So, to know that we've had a positive impact on people's lives... it's huge."

The shop's absence will leave behind more than just empty bookshelves, as it runs workshops and provides a sensory space.

Stephanie took her neurodivergent child to the shop and said the news was "truly heartbreaking" and that it would be an "immense loss" to Brentwood.

The 36-year-old teacher described it as an "incredible haven" of "knowledge, support and community".

"Natasha and her husband treated everyone who came into their shop as a close friend and went above and beyond to help," she said.

"Her love for children and their wellbeing was felt in every part of that shop and every club and session she ran."

Radford said her profit margins were thin, and a book she typically bought in at £4.05 would then sell for £6.99.

The business did not get the "deep discounts that the big boys get", she explained.

On top of that, she said her electricity bills had tripled since first opening, and that what she paid annually in business rates had increased from £2,868 in 2024 to £8,435 this year.

The amount many businesses are paying in rates has increased because the government reduced its temporary 75% "relief" discount to 40% in April 2025.

Rates are also dictated by market rental value, and Radford pointed out that this disproportionately affected a town close to London like Brentwood.

Radford said communities felt "fragmented" and allowing hubs to close was a "massive oversight" by the government.

An HM Treasury spokesperson told the BBC that the autumn Budget gave High Street businesses "more breathing space".

Traders will now only pay business rates once their rateable value reaches £18,000 - up from £12,000.

However, the spokesperson accepted that some areas were "more expensive than others", meaning certain shops would not benefit.

Rental value was a "commercial decision" between landlords and businesses, they added.

articles.title: Nagaland: Oxford museum returns ancestral  Naga skulls to India
articles.summary: The remains will be taken to Nagaland, where tribal leaders plan a joint memorial and burial.
articles.body:
The University of Oxford has returned the remains of 39 people taken from the Naga community during British colonial rule in India.

A delegation of around 30 people from Nagaland, a mountainous state in north-eastern India, attended a ceremony at Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum on Monday to mark the handover.

The remains, most of which are skulls, will be taken back to India and given what Naga tribal leaders have described as a "respectful rest". There are plans to bury them under a joint memorial in a park in Nagaland.

Museum director Laura Van Broekhoven described it as "a historic moment that will be part of stories told to next generations".

She said the remains were finally on their way home after overcoming "so much red tape everywhere".

The human remains were displayed at the Oxford museum for decades before being removed from public view in 2020 as part of what it described as a "decolonisation process".

The Pitt Rivers Museum holds more than 6,000 objects associated with Naga culture, believed to be the largest such collection in the world. Most were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar (the former Burma).

The museum's website lists 219 items as human remains.

These were added to the museum's collection between 1910 and 1940 and mostly collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.

The museum's website mentions that the objects collected during this period were "frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given".

During their visit to Oxford, the Naga delegation also met descendants of one of the anthropologists involved in collecting the remains.

"The manner in which these human remains were taken away from our land leaves much for us to speculate," one of the tribal leaders, Thejao Vihienuo, told AFP.

"I suspect that nobody would have given the skull of his father or his grandfather as a gift to another person."

Anthropologists say that the Naga people once practised head hunting, severing the heads of enemies as trophies. But they also kept the heads of their own chiefs at the centre of villages.

The Pitt Rivers Museum, founded in the 19th Century, has previously returned human remains to indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the US.

The latest handover to India concerns only the 39 ancestral remains and comes after a visit by a Naga delegation to Oxford in 2025, when it formally requested their return.

The museum had announced in September that the remains would be returned to India.

articles.title: The Gloucestershire swan sanctuary fighting climate change
articles.summary: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.
articles.body:
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.

Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).

Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.

Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."

WWT now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK.

Many people come to enjoy the swans, geese, flamingoes and migrating wildfowl, but do not realise how powerful these habitats can be in soaking up carbon and slowing down climate change.

So how vital are wetlands for birds, and how powerful can they be in the fight against climate change?

In November 1946, a naturalist called Peter Scott came to a wild marshy area on the banks of the River Severn, near Slimbridge. He was drawn by the thousands of migrating geese and swans that flew thousands of miles from the Russian Arctic to spend the winter here on the mudflats and marshes.

Captivated, Scott settled in a small cottage and later built a house right on a lake, with a huge window to watch the wildfowl.

He dug lakes and connecting channels, built hides and even towers to watch the birds without disturbing them.

Over the years, the reserve grew and became home to thousands of ducks, swans , geese as well as the migrating wildfowl.

"He really was a pioneer in conservation," said Chris Moore, a historian of Slimbridge and author of Peter Scott and the Birth of Modern Conservation.

As well as creating a safe haven for endangered species, Scott was a vigorous campaigner for nature.

He led the fight to stop commercial whaling, presented some of the BBC's first natural history programmes called live from Slimbridge, and helped set up WWF, the World Wildlife Fund.

In 1973 Sir Peter Scott became the first person to be knighted for conservation work.

Moore explained: "Scott was talking about the impact that man was having on the natural world, long before we started talking about climate change and global warming.

"David Attenborough called him the Patron Saint of Conservation, and I think that is more than deserved," Moore added.

Electrical items caused fatal fire, inquest hears

Residents protest against plans for greenbelt homes

One of Scott's typically ambitious projects was to save the Hawaiian Goose, or Nēnē.

Unique to the Pacific islands, the Nēnē was hit hard by road building and development. By 1949 barely 24 birds remained.

Scott heard of its plight, and asked Hawaiian authorities to send a few geese to Slimbridge where he hand-reared them.

"Unfortunately they sent us two females," chuckled Enid Cole, a WWT volunteer at Slimbridge.

"Peter asked them for a gander - 'It would help', he said."

Nine chicks were later born, and hand-raised successfully to adulthood at Slimbridge.

Today there are more than 3,000 Nēnē geese, most of them living peacefully on Hawaiian golf courses. But a handful still live at Slimbridge, where Enid Cole and her friends hand feed them lettuce every day.

"It's a marvelous project, and typical of Sir Peter," Enid smiled.

Over the last 80 years, the teams at Slimbridge have hand-reared several other species, including the Common Crane and the world's rarest diving duck, the Madagascan Pochard.

It was while they were working to save the Madagascan Pochard that they realised how vital the wetland habitats were.

"We realised that to save that species, we had to bring the wetland back," explained Sarah Fowler, WWT's chief executive.

"And to bring the wetland back, we had to work with the whole community in Madagascar."

Ian Hollister, a volunteer warden at Slimbridge, said: "The wetlands are great at absorbing carbon, they're like a soggy secret weapon."

Scientists calculate that 85% of the world's wetland habitats have been lost as marshes drained for agriculture, and swamps cleared for construction as cities expand.

And yet, as Fowler explained, "40% of the world's species rely on wetland habitats for survival".

What started at Slimbridge has spread to 10 wetland reserves across the UK with the charity now working with local councils to restore wetlands, even in small city areas.

A scheme in Bristol has seen small floating islands of wetland plants moored in the city's harbour.

Across the world, they are campaigning to restore one million hectares of lost wetland, partly to provide safe habitats for endangered species but also because wetlands help absorb carbon far quicker than even forests.

"Salt marshes bury carbon," said Fowler.

"Every time the big tides go over them, the plants that have grown up in the salt marsh get buried. Those plants are full of carbon, so they are a massive carbon sink.

"And the brilliant thing about salt marshes is they do this four times faster than trees. Wetlands are vital in our fight against climate change, and we must restore them."

What started 80 years ago as a bird reserve on the banks of a river in Gloucestershire has grown into a global campaign to restore wetlands, which they call the "soggy secret weapon" against climate change.

articles.title: A Missouri county sought bids for public land beside a golf course, alarming residents who use the forest and trails; after a wave of protests, officials canceled the sale process on November 9
articles.summary: Jackson County in Missouri has cancelled its request for bids on public land along the Blue River Parkway after residents and conservation groups opposed
articles.body: Jackson County in Missouri has cancelled its request for bids on public land along the Blue River Parkway after residents and conservation groups opposed the proposed sale. The decision was made on Monday, a day before the deadline for submitting bids.The county had invited proposals for land near Hillcrest Golf Course, raising concerns among people who regularly visit the area, Axios reported. The property has natural-surface trails used for hiking and mountain biking. Volunteers have also worked on building and maintaining these trails for several years.The proposed sale led to objections from local residents, outdoor enthusiasts and environmental organisations. They questioned why the county was considering selling land that was part of a larger protected parkway and used for recreational activities.County Executive Phil LeVota announced that the bidding process had been closed and that the county would not proceed with the proposed sale. The announcement also confirmed that no legislative action on the sale would be considered at the Jackson County Legislative meeting on November 9.Why the county had sought bidsThe proposal began after representatives of Hillcrest Country Club approached the county about using land along the Blue River to expand the golf course. The country club had been temporarily closed at the time.At an August 3 meeting of the County Legislature, LeVota said the request for bids followed the golf course's interest in the property. The county then started a process to invite proposals from potential buyers.According to the county, the land was included in the surplus property process to understand whether there was interest from potential buyers and to explore possible future uses.A resolution supporting the bidding process stated that "the Administration can identify no current or future use for the property". LeVota also said during the meeting that the land had been sitting empty for decades.However, the proposal drew objections from people who said the area was not unused. They pointed to the trails and other outdoor activities that regularly take place there.The property consisted of three existing parcels along the Blue River, south of Swope Park and east of Hillcrest Golf Course. It lies north of the Blue River Glades Natural Area, which is protected by the Missouri Department of Conservation. The land is also within the county-protected Blue River Parkway.Residents, conservation groups oppose The proposed sale brought objections from residents and several organisations, including Bridging the Gap, Heartland Conservation Alliance and Urban Trail Co.The organisations raised concerns about the future of the trails and natural areas. Urban Trail Co. maintains trails in the Blue River Glades area, where volunteers have helped develop routes for outdoor activities.The Blue River Parkway covers 2,267 acres and is the largest park managed by Jackson County. Its management is guided by the Blue River Parkway Master Plan, which was passed in 2022.According to Scott Capstack, a founding member of Heartland Outside, volunteers began building natural-surface trails in the area as early as 2000. An official trail partnership with Jackson County started in 2006.The work resulted in more than eight miles of trails for hiking and mountain biking. These routes are also promoted on the county's website.Capstack said the trails attract visitors regularly. "That's used, I would say, every day," he said as quoted by Martic City Telegraph.Trail users argued that the land had recreational value and should not be treated as unused property. Their concerns also focused on the possibility that future development could affect access to the trails.'Protected areas were never meant to be sold'While announcing the cancellation, LeVota said some natural features of the area were never part of the proposed sale."We were never proposing to sell the glades, trails, or the areas we intended to preserve," he said in the county's November 9 announcement. "I want residents to understand that protecting those areas was always part of the plan," he added.LeVota said the county had included the property in the surplus process to examine possible interest and future uses. He added that there was no reason to continue with the bidding process.The county also said some people had accessed the property without proper authorisation. According to its statement, people had been creating trails and cutting down trees without the owner's consent.The county described this as a liability concern and said it could not be held responsible for changes made to the land without its approval.Ben Reed, who previously led Urban Trail Co., disputed the suggestion that the volunteers lacked permission to manage the trails. He told Axios that the organisation had an agreement signed with the county in 2018, allowing its volunteers to carry out land management work.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: DR Congo conflict: At least 66 Congolese soldiers sentenced to death for cowardice
articles.summary: The Congolese army's fight against rebel groups has long been hampered by disarray within its ranks.
articles.body:
At least 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in the Democratic Republic of Congo for cowardice, mutiny and refusing to obey orders, local media report.

The sentences followed a trial of 71 soldiers before a military court in Walikale, in North Kivu province, in eastern DR Congo. Four soldiers were acquitted, while another was sentenced to 10 years in prison.

The army said the trial was intended to improve discipline among troops as they battle armed groups in eastern DR Congo.

The region has endured decades of conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition that includes the M23 group.

The soldiers were reportedly arrested on 20 October in Walikale, where they were accused of abandoning their positions and fleeing during clashes with FRN fighters.

The Congolese army's campaign against armed groups, including the M23, has long been undermined by poor discipline and disorganisation within its ranks.

The government has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23, an allegation denied by both Kigali and the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.

The army has faced persistent criticism over its lack of professionalism and disciplined, while soldiers have complained of poor pay and inadequate equipment.

Last month, another 27 soldiers were sentenced to death on similar charges of cowardice after reportedly withdrawing from the frontline during clashes with rebels.

In March 2024, DR Congo lifted a 20-year moratorium on the death penalty, citing the need to remove "traitors" within the army.

The government said capital punishment would also apply to people involved in armed groups, insurrection, as well as committing treason and war crimes.

The decision to reinstate the death penalty was widely criticised by rights groups. However, no formal executions have been carried out since the moratorium was lifted.

Since the beginning of 2025, at least 507 soldiers have been convicted, including 381 death sentences, according to figures compiled by French broadcaster RFI.

In October 2025, former Congolese President Joseph Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself. He has since been named as the FRN's leader.

articles.title: Meghan makes first public appearance since father's arrest
articles.summary: The Duchess of Sussex had pulled out of giving a speech with Prince Harry at the event promoting children's online safety.
articles.body:
The Duchess of Sussex has made her first public appearance since her father was charged with possession of child sex abuse material.

Meghan joined her husband Prince Harry at the European Parliament in Brussels on Tuesday, where he delivered a speech calling for greater protection for children online.

Harry gave the keynote address alone after Meghan reportedly withdrew from speaking alongside him because she did not feel emotionally strong enough.

The duchess was seen holding her husband's hand tightly as they arrived at the Paul-Henri Spaak building. She did not respond to questions from reporters about how she was feeling.

During his speech, Harry said he and his wife stood alongside parents who had lost children to online harm.

"I'm not here as an expert or a politician. I'm here as a father. My wife, a mother," he told the European Parliament.

The duke stressed the importance of preventing online harm and said children "deserve to feel safe wherever they are", including in classrooms and playgrounds.

He did not reference Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, who appeared in court in Florida on Friday charged with possession of child sex abuse images.

Markle, who is currently under home detention and subject to electronic monitoring, has previously denied the allegations.

Meghan has been estranged from her father for several years. He did not attend her wedding in Windsor in 2018 citing "ill health" at the time.

When reports emerged about Thomas Markle last month, including allegations he possessed child sex abuse images, Meghan released a statement saying she was "deeply distressed at the news" and hoped that "justice will be fully served".

Compared with her public appearance in Nottingham last month , today's event was a quieter, more subdued affair, with Meghan holding her husband's hand throughout.

Sources close to the couple say the past few weeks have been emotionally challenging.

But online safety remains an important part of their campaigning, and it's understood the duchess felt it was important to attend in support of families affected.

"I'm not asking for a world without technology," Prince Harry said, as he called for stronger safety measures and a greater focus on prevention.

Following his speech, the duke also took part in a panel discussion, where he described the addictive nature of social media as "brainwashing on an extraordinary scale".

He said everyone had a responsibility to protect children from companies that "clearly don't care", adding that a "handful of very powerful people" wanted to see a social media world characterised by "lawlessness, little consequence, complete chaos (and) division".

Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge

The duke and duchess's appearance marked the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial which has moved to Europe after being launched in New York last year.

Supported by their Archewell charity, the memorial features a moving collection of images of young people whose parents believe their deaths were linked to linked to harm they had experienced on social media. Each image is a photo of a son or daughter that a mum or dad held in their phone.

The memorial includes a photo of 13-year-old Breck Bednar from Surrey, who died in 2014. His parents believe he was groomed online via gaming and social media apps.

Another image shows Jools Sweeney from Gloucestershire, who took his own life in 2022. His parents say his use of social media during the Covid lockdown contributed to his death.

BBC Breakfast spoke to Harry and Meghan in April last year when the Lost Screen Memorial first went on display in New York.

"No matter how polarised the world is," Meghan told the BBC, "one thing we can all agree on is that our children should be safe, all of our children should be safe".

The couple want their campaign to put pressure on social media companies to better support families following the loss of a child.

"These companies are getting away with it by saying we don't need to give you disclosure," an emotional Prince Harry told BBC Breakfast last year.

"You're telling a parent, you're telling a Dad and a Mum that they can't have the details of what their kid was up to on social media because of the privacy of their kid - the parents who've seen their kid from the time they were a child. It's wrong."

articles.title: Stroud locals launch campaign to buy Ruscombe Wood
articles.summary: Locals have a year to raise the money needed to buy Ruscombe Wood near Stroud.
articles.body:
Local villagers are hoping to buy an ancient woodland so it can be saved from private sale and continue to be a sanctuary for generations to come.

Landowners Margaret and David Lloyd have allowed the public to enjoy their 17-acre Ruscombe Wood near Stroud for the last 20 years but have now decided to sell up.

Keen for it to go into the hands of local residents, the couple have given Ruscombe Woodlands Committee one year to raise £164,000 to cover purchase, legal and survey costs.

Martin Humphreys from the committee said: "I like the idea that if we own the woods, nature will become part of the community and we can have that instead of a community hall."

Electrical items caused fatal fire, inquest hears

No work on cycle stretch until review - council

The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change

Made up of local residents, the committee have now launched a fundraising campaign to raise the funds for the purchase and said it hopes to protect wildlife and habitat, along with guaranteeing permissive footpaths at the site continue to stay open for everyone.

It also hopes to offer free workshops, including on woodland care, natural skills and creative crafts.

Margaret, 79, said they had decided it was time to sell their "pretty special piece of ancient woodland" after realising it had become "too much work" for them.

"We want the community to buy it because they all love it and we want it loved like we've loved it all this time," she said.

"Really, we'd like it sold now and we could put it back on the market, but it wouldn't be the same, so the only snag for us is that it wont get done until November 2027," she added.

Margaret said the group also have plans to use the space as a forest school.

Martin said it was "very nice" that the couple had given them time to raise the money needed for the purchase.

He said while the group has to get through a lot of legalities, he likes the idea that the woodland could eventually be owned by everybody.

"It has no public rights of way, it's not been spoilt or overworked, it's wild and has lots of creatures that have made their homes there.

"It has a wonderful silent quality," Humphreys added.

articles.title: 28-Day Challenge: A heart scan made me give up everything I loved. Today I eat Nutella crêpes
articles.summary: In August 2015, my wife insisted I get a heart scan. I was 43.
articles.body: In August 2015, my wife insisted I get a heart scan. I was 43. I played soccer every week, I looked fit, and my cholesterol reports had told me for years that all was well.The score came back 266. My arteries had more calcium than those of 98 out of 100 men my age. I had heart disease, and I had felt nothing at all.So I did what frightened people do. I cut out all sugar. I slashed my carbs. Within three months, my markers were far better. I joked to my wife that if living longer was the goal, I had achieved it, because those three months felt like three years.I knew I could not live like that for the rest of my life. So I asked a different question. What is the least I can give up and still get the result?Eleven years as my own lab ratI began testing my blood every three months. I wore every device I could find and worked closely with doctors and dietitians. I tested when I ate, how much protein I had, when I exercised, even when I showered.Some experiments were miserable. I once fasted for 72 hours. My data showed nothing a 24-hour fast had not already given me, and it hurt my muscle mass. Out it went.What survived would disappoint most influencers. No peptides. Mostly things our grandmothers told us. I even had to eat salad, which I had always thought was for cows.The crêpe experimentThen came my favourite test. I wore a glucose monitor for two weeks, which shows your blood sugar through the day, and tried about 39 meals.At one of my favourite restaurants, on a day with little exercise, I ate a big green salad with no dressing. Then a Nutella and berries crêpe. I waited for my blood sugar to shoot up.Two hours later, the line was still pretty flat. I felt I had unlocked a magic spell.The post meal walk surprised me just as much. After a plate of rice and dal, if I walked, my blood sugar stopped at about 113 or 114. On days I sat still, on purpose, for the experiment, it could reach 160, 170, even 180.I asked my sister to put on the continuous glucose monitor so she could see it for herself. Weeks after it came off, she told me I had permanently embedded it in her brain. Once you see that graph, you can’t unsee it.To be fair, I am one person, not a clinical trial. Your numbers may differ, especially if you have diabetes. Nutella is a processed food, and I don’t have it every day. And none of this replaces medicine: I also take a statin, as my doctors advised.But in my blood test this June, my numbers were much better than they were at the end of that three-month diet.I have written more than 80 blog posts about all this. People were wonderfully kind about them, but then very little changed. The most common reaction was some version of “What an amazing guy” or “wow, you are so disciplined” vs I had hoped for them saying “I can do this too.”This led to the creation of the 28-Day ChallengeWe start with 3 questions:What will you never give up? Mine are my Nutella crêpe, my Ghirardelli ice cream and soccer, though doctors have suggested I stop soccer after my injuries. Some of my friends won’t give up their glass of Scotch. You don’t have to justify yours to anyone; just have clarity on what yours are.What are you happy to give up? I never drank much, so alcohol was easy to reduce / stop.What are you willing to add? For me: salad, strength training and a walk after meals.That is the trade. It is not a sacrifice if YOU choose it.We then get started with four small habits, one a week, done together on WhatsApp. Each week we had a presentation on the science and practical habits from our team of expert dietitians. We provided a daily task that ramped up in scope so each of the four interventions slowly but surely became a habit. Community members posted photos of their meals, their walks, their protein combinations, etc.In October, we asked members in a poll what helped them most. Seeing their peers post their plates, share their struggles and their wins, and encouragement to each other, stole the show. And the results they shared with us reflected this.At the end of the 28 days, 94% said salad first was now part of their day, and 82% said the same of the walk after meals. In addition, 67% of the members said they felt more energy, 57% felt lighter with less bloating, and 42% said their clothes fit better. In just those 28 days, the average reduction in waist circumference was 2.2 cm, and average weight across was down about 1 kg. This is just the beginning.Eleven years of my data, and what moved people was someone else’s lunch. As a few members put it:“Knowing and actually practicing them every day are two very different things.”“Now, if I don’t walk after a meal, it feels like something is missing. If I don’t eat my salad before the meal, it feels incomplete.”“I feel more confident, energetic and enthusiastic throughout the day and I am in love with this improved version of myself.”“When I started the challenge, I must admit I was quite sceptical. The four habits seemed like simple common sense – things I already knew... But I couldn’t have been more wrong!... More than just reinforcing what I knew, you helped me understand how to actually put it into practice.”The next round starts Monday, November 16. It costs Rs 999 in India and $49 elsewhere. Join us here at If you don’t, I have one request. Before you make your next health promise, decide this first: what is your Nutella crêpe?(Nickhil Jakatdar, PhD, is the CEO of GenePath Diagnostics and the co-founder and chairman of PreventiveHealth.ai, which runs the 28-Day Challenge. This is general education, not medical advice. Please talk to your doctor before changing your diet or medication.)Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash
articles.summary: The contents of the calendar, including hair clips and keychains, have been widely criticised on social media.
articles.body:
Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.

The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.

A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products".

The BBC has contacted Skims for comment.

The shapewear and clothing business was co-founder by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine.

Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.

One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".

A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.

articles.title: 'Tipu fought 4 Anglo-Mysore wars; RSS skipped freedom struggle': Karnataka minister Priyank Kharge
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Karnataka home minister Priyank Kharge on Tuesday defended Tipu Sultan, saying that while the former Mysore ruler fought four Anglo-Mysore
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Karnataka home minister Priyank Kharge on Tuesday defended Tipu Sultan, saying that while the former Mysore ruler fought four Anglo-Mysore Wars, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) had "no role in India's freedom struggle.""The BJP needs to get its history right. Tipu Sultan fought four Anglo-Mysore Wars. The RSS did not even participate in the freedom struggle. They did not take part in the Civil Disobedience Movement, Quit India Movement, Dandi March or Non-Cooperation Movement, nor were they involved in any of the Round Table Conferences. They did nothing, yet they are the ones dictating terms," Priyank Kharge, son of Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, told reporters.The RSS is the ideological mentor of the BJP, which is the principal opposition party in Karnataka and has been India's governing party since 2014.The Congress leader also cited a book in which senior BJP leader and former Karnataka chief minister BS Yediyurappa had praised Tipu Sultan, accusing the BJP of engaging in "pure opportunistic politics". Priyank Kharge alleged that the saffron party adopts a pro-minority stance while seeking votes but changes its position after elections.Also Read | 'Double standards': Congress posts ex-President Ramnath Kovind’s video ‘praising’ Tipu Sultan"The BJP opposed Tipu Jayanti when Yediyurappa ji was the chief minister, yet he had praised Tipu Sultan in a book. You cannot erase Tipu Sultan's contributions to the state. This is nothing but politics. When they want votes, they become pro-minority; when they don't, they behave differently. The government will take a decision. You cannot simply erase history, whether you like it or not," he added.His remarks came after cultural organisation Tehrik-e-Khudadad submitted a memorandum to Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar, urging the state government to reinstate the official celebration of Tipu Sultan Jayanti on November 10.The organisation also called on the authorities to review school textbooks to ensure that Tipu Sultan and his father, Hyder Ali, receive what it described as "historically accurate" coverage.The proposal is currently pending before the Chief Minister's Office.Tipu Sultan Jayanti was first introduced in 2015 by the Congress government led by then chief minister Siddaramaiah. articles.title: Cost of living: £250 help with heating bills in Wales
articles.summary: Households dependent on either heating oil or LPG and are eligible for reduced council tax will benefit.
articles.body:
Up to 20,000 homes using heating oil could get a £250 payment from the Welsh government to help with the rising cost of living.

The government said £5m from a new £130m package will help "off grid" households who are dependent on either heating oil or LPG and are eligible for reduced council tax.

The package includes the £100 household energy payment, with this extended to those eligible for council tax relief "irrespective of band".

It also includes £7m support for bus travel and £8m for councils to help those "not captured by other schemes".

It follows the UK government unveiling a £100 "household energy payment" for council taxpayers in bands A-D in England in October.

Wales' Deputy First Minister Sioned Williams said supporting families with the cost of living was a "key priority".

"We understand that this is a challenging time for many households across Wales," she said.

"In total this represents an additional investment of £130m, providing immediate relief for households this winter. While we are taking firm action wherever we can, we need the UK Government to play its part".

Five million pounds of the package will help towards "off-grid" fuel costs with a £250 payment available to households eligible for Council Tax Reduction based on their incomes and are dependent on either heating oil or LPG.

An additional £8m will allow councils to extend the £100 payment to households "not captured" by other schemes and are facing financial hardship.

While £7m is being made available to support bus operators with their high fuel costs and protect passengers from fares increases.

The Welsh government said with winter approaching and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East , "the coming months will be a challenging time for many".

"This package represents a significant investment in Welsh communities and reflects our determination to stand alongside households during challenging times," it added.

The Welsh government had already said it would make the £100 energy payment to about one million households in Wales following Chancellor John Healey's UK Budget announcement in October.

The chancellor said council taxpayers in bands A-D in England would get the payment and urged the Welsh government to follow his lead, with Wales' Finance Minister Elin Jones subsequently saying households in the same bands in Wales would also benefit.

Healey announced an end to gas standing charges but did not address call to help those people, mainly in rural areas, who relied on either heating oil or LPG.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine and US meet for Abu Dhabi talks as Trump says war can 'end soon'
articles.summary: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has been ongoing for 1,721 days.
articles.body:
American, Ukrainian and Russian representatives gathered in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their latest round of trilateral peace talks, with President Donald Trump's administration seeking a diplomatic breakthrough after 1,721 days of Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor.

Trump -- who came to office vowing to end the war within 24 hours -- has thus far been unable to force a breakthrough. His chief negotiating envoys, Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, are leading the U.S. delegation in Abu Dhabi this week.

On Monday, Trump struck a positive tone when discussing the coming meeting. "They talk about wars, Ukraine and Russia. And by the way, we're having a very good conversation about that in Abu Dhabi," the president said.

"Ukraine and Russia are tired of fighting. They're tired of seeing dead young soldiers," Trump added.

A source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office told ABC News that Kyiv's delegation is led by Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service and its lead representative in previous rounds of talks . Among those accompanying him are Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Zelenskyy's office, and Davyd Arakhamia, the head of Zelenskyy's party in the Ukrainian parliament.

The Russian delegation is led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said. Also attending are Kremlin official Yuri Ushakov, the head of Russia's foreign military intelligence agency, Igor Kostyukov, and Sergei Ryabkov, the deputy foreign minister, Peskov said.

The first U.S.-brokered trilateral meeting was held in Geneva in February 2026, but this year has seen little diplomatic progress, with both camps still far apart on key issues. The negotiations have secured some prisoner-of-war exchanges and short-lived, localized ceasefires.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Monday that this week's talks will put "security issues concerning Russia, Ukraine and the region as a whole" at the top of the agenda. The participants would also work toward "agreeing on principles that could be approved following consultations on a comprehensive settlement of the conflict in Ukraine," Lavrov said.

Zelenskyy said Monday that he had spoken with European Commission President Ursula von Der Leyen ahead of the talks. Both the French and German foreign ministers also said they would be participating in the Abu Dhabi meetings, though Peskov maintained that the talks would remain trilateral in format.

A statement posted to the Ukrainian presidential website said Kyiv "is doing everything to ensure that the trilateral format delivers results."

Delegation head Umerov, meanwhile, said in a post to Telegram on Tuesday morning that Kyiv's team is prioritizing "ending hostilities, reliable post-war security guarantees, economic recovery and development of Ukraine, and humanitarian measures."

With the war approaching its fifth anniversary, the two combatants appear far apart on a potential settlement. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly rejected U.S.-Ukrainian proposals for a ceasefire under which a final settlement could be negotiated.

Moscow is demanding that Ukraine withdraw from four contested regions -- Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson -- the Kremlin claimed to have annexed in September 2022, after referendums that the international community largely refused to recognize. Putin also wants Ukraine permanently barred from NATO and to face limits on the size and capabilities of its military.

Zelenskyy has said Ukraine cannot agree to any deal that does not include concrete security guarantees from the U.S. and other NATO allies to protect against renewed Russian aggression.

Kyiv, Zelenskyy said, must also retain the right to constitute its own armed forces and choose its own future security arrangements, including membership of NATO. The Ukrainian leader has refused Russian demands to cede territory not controlled by Moscow's forces.

Since Trump returned to office, U.S.-Ukrainian ties have at times been fraught. The president has repeatedly pressured Zelenskyy to make concessions to Moscow in pursuit of a peace deal. Trump has described Zelenskyy at times as a "dictator" and criticized Kyiv for delaying planned elections, which constitutionally cannot be held while the country is under martial law.

Trump has suspended U.S. financial and military aid to Ukraine, instead demanding that other NATO allies purchase American arms intended for Ukraine's use. Kyiv has repeatedly appealed to the U.S. to provide more ammunition for its Patriot surface-to-air missile systems in particular, the systems key to Ukrainian efforts to blunt escalating Russian drone and ballistic missile strikes.

In March, Trump threatened to expand sanctions and tariffs on Russia in a bid to push Moscow to the negotiating table. Ultimately Trump failed to do so, and in the lead-up to this month's midterm elections struck a deal with Putin to import cargoes of Russian diesel -- a move that prompted criticism from domestic opponents, foreign allies and Kyiv.

Trump told CBS News' "60 Minutes" program on Sunday that he still believes an agreement to end Russia's full-scale invasion is possible. "I believe that that war is going to end and it's going to end soon. And the only reason it's going to end is because of me," Trump said.

Trump also appeared to imply that he was open to changes in Ukraine's borders as part of a peace agreement, saying that the country will end up with "a little bit different shape Ukraine."

Trump said the enmity between Putin and Zelenskyy was the prime obstacle to a deal: "There's tremendous hatred," he said. Asked whether that sentiment is understandable coming from Zelenskyy, given that his country was invaded, Trump said it is, but also suggested that Ukraine had disrespected Russia during an initial meeting.

"Well, it is, but when they had their first meeting, there was great disrespect shown to Russia. So I'm not going to say," Trump said. Asked if he thought Putin was stringing him along, Trump replied, "Oh, I don't think so."

A U.S. official told ABC News during a briefing on Monday that negotiators were "cautiously optimistic" ahead of the talks in Abu Dhabi, though framed the meeting as a jumping off point for more complex negotiations to end the war.

"While both parties remain skeptical of the other party's intentions, we do see promising signs as the mediator, and we're going to work to keep pushing to build the areas of common ground so that we can work to a conclusion," the U.S. official said.

Trump's comments and conduct have deepened concerns in Ukraine that the president wants the victims of the war, rather than the aggressors, to pay the price for peace, Oleksandr Merezhko -- a member of the Ukrainian parliament and the chair of the body's foreign affairs committee -- told ABC News.

Merezhko said he has "absolutely no hopes" for this week's meetings in Abu Dhabi, beyond possible new deals to exchange prisoners of war. "There can't be any tangible result because Putin keeps insisting on his absurd demands which, in reality, mean surrender for Ukraine," he said.

"Putin's goal is to imitate negotiations to avoid sanctions from Trump. But he has absolutely no intent to negotiate with a goal to reach a concrete result," Merezhko suggested. "His ultimate goal is not a ceasefire or a compromise; his goal is subjection of Ukraine and installment in Kyiv of a Russian puppet regime."

Both Russian and American officials have said that the Abu Dhabi talks will include discussions on broader European security arrangements. That "seems to be new," said Samuel Charap, a senior political scientist at RAND who has advocated for talks.

Still, Charap told ABC News, "They're not going to come to some radically more ambitious agreement given there hasn't been any conversation for the past nine months."

Putin launched the invasion in February 2022 with the intention of dismembering Ukraine and installing a pliant government in Kyiv. The "special military operation," as the Kremlin termed the assault, marked the latest chapter in Moscow's decades-long effort to retain influence over Kyiv and undermine Ukraine's relations with the European Union and NATO.

What the Kremlin intended as a short campaign has now lasted longer than either World War I or the Soviet Union's confrontation with Nazi Germany in World War II, known in Russia as Great Patriotic War.

Russian officials routinely describe the war with Ukraine as a direct contest with the NATO alliance, whose constituent nations rallied to support Ukraine military and financially, added two new members -- Sweden and Finland -- and sought to increase collective military spending to meet the Russian threat.

Fierce fighting continues all along the 745-mile frontline. The invasion quickly devolved into a bloody war of attrition, with Russian units edging forward -- at massive cost, according to figures published by the Ukrainian military and broadly supported by Western intelligence assessments -- along the contact line in parts of eastern and southeastern Ukraine.

This year has seen significant Ukrainian counterattacks in the contested Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, liberating hundreds of miles of occupied territory, according to commanders in Kyiv.

Meanwhile, both Russia and Ukraine have expanded their long-range strike campaigns through the course of 2026. Each night, hundreds and sometimes thousands of drones and missiles cross the shared border heading in both directions, with Kyiv and Moscow both among the regular targets.

The number of civilian casualties is steadily creeping up as a result, particularly among Ukrainians.

Overnight into Tuesday, Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 162 drones, of which 96 were jet-powered, and one ballistic missile into the country. The air force said that 135 drones, of which 70 were jet-powered, were shot down or otherwise suppressed. Impacts were reported across 19 locations, the air force said.

Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said its forces downed at least 155 Ukrainian drones overnight.

ABC News' Victoria Beaule, Oleksiy Pshemyskyi, Natalia Kushnir, Tanya Stukalova, Anna Sergeeva, Shannon K. Kington and Michelle Stoddart contributed to this report.

articles.title: Edinburgh Academy pupils suffered decades of 'dreadful abuse'
articles.summary: A report from the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry says the school focused on protecting its reputation and ignored complaints.
articles.body:
Pupils at Edinburgh Academy suffered decades of "dreadful abuse", a report has found.

Lady Smith, who chairs the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry (SCAI), details more than 40 years of sexual, physical, and emotional abuse at the school in her latest report .

She says the school focused on protecting its reputation and ignored complaints.

Lady Smith also names four serial perpetrators of the abuse, including two who went on to offend at other schools.

Edinburgh Academy, which had previously apologised for "brutal and unrestrained" historical abuse , said it was committed to facing up to "the wrongs of the past".

The inquiry heard claims of historical abuse against 20 teaching staff at the private school, with most of the evidence covering the years between 1954 and 1995.

Nearly 50 witnesses gave evidence, including broadcaster Nicky Campbell - who said one teacher had abused children on an "industrial scale".

Edinburgh Academy apologises for 'brutal' abuse

Nicky Campbell claims 'Savile scale' teacher abuse

'I can't bear his blood in me' - sex abuser's daughter

Publishing her findings, former judge Lady Smith said the school had "failed to look at itself through a realistic and critical lens" for decades.

"It is clear it was assumed that abuse did not and would not take place," she said.

"When it did, the school could not accept that it had happened, failed to address it, and failed to recognise the risk of it continuing. Complacency was the order of the day.

"When complaints were made, they were either disbelieved or left unresolved. Staff chose not to notice and avoided intervention or investigation despite there being obvious signs of abuse."

The report names two long-serving members of staff as perpetrator of abuse: Hamish Dawson , a housemaster and senior school teacher, and John Brownlee , a housemaster and deputy head of the junior school.

It also singles out prep school teacher Iain Wares , who went on to abuse pupils at Fettes College and is currently awaiting extradition from South Africa; and physics teacher William Bain , who has twice been convicted of sex offences.

He began his lengthy history of abuse at Edinburgh Academy before moving on to harm children in other schools.

The report highlights the evidence of one pupil, who used the pseudonym Henry. He spent nine years at the school and said abuse was part of daily life.

He told the inquiry it was normal for 11-year-olds to be groomed with jelly babies, and for them to be molested in front of other pupils.

"It was normal to kick, hit, and strangle, to the point of unconsciousness, 10-year-olds. It was normal to inflict physical punishment with a plank of wood with no good reason."

He said grown men subjected children to "psychological belittlement" and that "endless cycles of bullying" went unnoticed or unchecked.

Henry said "flagrant racism, sexism, homophobia" was ignored and there was no safeguarding.

"It was normal for there to be no pastoral care, and it was normal to be somewhere where nobody, not one person, loved or genuinely cared for you," he added.

Lady Smith said: 'None of this behaviour was "normal". Or acceptable. It was simply abusive.'"

The report said as recently as 2001 the school's Court of Directors focused its reputation and how it was perceived, rather than how life actually was for its pupils.

Lady Smith said Hamish Dawson's "eccentric" classroom behaviour was known about and yet "celebrated by the school".

Various "instruments of correction" which he had used to abuse pupils were auctioned on his departure from the school.

The report said sexual abuse extended over four decades, from the 1950s to the 1980s, and included instances of children sexually abusing other children.

Physical abuse was "normalised" and children in the Prep School were regularly beaten until corporal punishment was abolished in1988.

Following the introduction of co-education in the sixth form, girls were the targets of "unpleasant and abusive misogyny".

The report found there was no evidence that the school gave any consideration to the obvious risks involved.

The Edinburgh Academy Survivors Group welcomed the findings and thanked the Lady Smith for an "accurate and thoughtful account of the events we endured as children".

The school's rector, Barry Welsh, said it had an "unwavering" commitment to facing up to "the wrongs of the past".

He said Lady Smith's report made for "sombre reading", and "reinforces the remarkable bravery shown by our former pupils who have given evidence.

"We reiterate our sincere apology to all those affected by any abuse that occurred at our school."

Welsh acknowledged the school could not change the past but pledged to "shape the future".

He added: "We continue to support survivors as fully as we are able whilst also educating our current pupils in a caring and supportive environment."

The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry was set up in October 2015 to look at the abuse of children in care in Scotland.

Lady Smith has previously produced reports on abuse carried out at a number of schools, children's homes and orphanages.

The Edinburgh Academy report was based on evidence hearings which took place between November 2021 and August 2023.

articles.title: Mystery threat puts US bases in Britain on high alert, aircraft shifted
articles.summary: A sudden security escalation at two major US military bases in Britain has triggered questions over a possible threat to American forces in Europe.
articles.body: A sudden security escalation at two major US military bases in Britain has triggered questions over a possible threat to American forces in Europe. US authorities have raised the alert level at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath to the second-highest security category, while several military aircraft have unexpectedly moved out of Mildenhall.According to a report by The War Zone (TWZ), the US military confirmed enhanced force protection measures at the two installations on November 9 but did not disclose what prompted the decision.A subsequent Wall Street Journal report, said both bases had been placed under Force Protection Condition Charlie (FPCON Charlie), a level activated when intelligence indicates terrorist activity is likely.The development comes amid renewed concerns over Iran-linked threats against American military installations overseas, following a security incident near another US-operated airbase in Britain earlier this year.In September 2026, British authorities arrested five men near RAF Fairford after three vans were found in the vicinity of the military installation. Although no explosives were discovered, the investigation subsequently led to two further arrests. One suspect was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service believed by British police to be Iran.The incident raised concerns about possible Iranian intelligence operations targeting US military assets in Britain. Tehran has denied involvement in the alleged plot.RAF Fairford had previously been used by American B-1B Lancer strategic bombers during military operations against Iran. The US subsequently withdrew the bombers from the installation amid concerns about potential threats.Unexpected aircraft movements from MildenhallThe latest security escalation coincided with unusual movements of American military aircraft from RAF Mildenhall.Flight-tracking observers reported that several KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refuelling aircraft were moved to other European locations, including Germany, Spain and Scotland. CV-22B Osprey special operations aircraft were also relocated from Mildenhall to RAF Lakenheath.According to subsequent reporting by Sky News, nine KC-135 tankers and three Ospreys were involved in the movements.The US Air Force said aircraft routinely move between installations for operational requirements and training. However, it did not establish whether these particular relocations were directly connected to the heightened security alert.RAF Mildenhall is a major American military hub in Britain. It hosts KC-135 Stratotankers, which extend the operational range of US fighter jets and bombers through aerial refuelling. The installation also houses RC-135 Rivet Joint reconnaissance aircraft, which collect intelligence and monitor military activity, alongside special operations aircraft.RAF Lakenheath, meanwhile, hosts F-15E Strike Eagle fighter-bombers and F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters. It is one of the most important US fighter installations in Europe and provides Washington with significant combat air capabilities in the region.Drone threat raises fresh concerns over US basesThe latest security alert has also drawn attention to the possibility of unmanned aerial systems being used to surveil or threaten American military installations in Britain. The concern is not without precedent.In November 2024, unidentified drones were repeatedly spotted flying near and over four UK airbases hosting US forces, including RAF Lakenheath, RAF Mildenhall, RAF Feltwell and RAF Fairford.The issue remains relevant because small drones can potentially be used to monitor aircraft movements, map security arrangements and gather intelligence around sensitive military infrastructure. Depending on their capabilities and payloads, they can also pose risks to flight operations and personnel.The possibility of such activity has resurfaced after RAF Lakenheath issued a public warning on November 9, urging residents to report suspicious activity, including unauthorised drone operations, around the installation.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Why are we becoming Vishwaguru in air pollution?' Congress questions PM Modi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Tuesday targeted the BJP-led government at the Centre over rising air pollution in Delhi, asking why
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Tuesday targeted the BJP-led government at the Centre over rising air pollution in Delhi, asking why the national capital was becoming a “Vishwaguru” in pollution.In a post on X, Kharge said that clean air is a fundamental right, not a privilege to be granted by the Government.“Why are we becoming a ‘Vishwaguru’ in air pollution? Piecemeal measures, PR stunts, broken promises and blame games have become the hallmark of the BJP,” he said.Delhi has been witnessing deteriorating air quality following Diwali, with pollution from multiple sources, including stubble burning in neighbouring states, adding to the crisis.Kharge flags missing PM2.5 readings at 36 monitoring stationsThe Congress chief alleged that discrepancies in air quality monitoring had raised further questions over the government's handling of pollution.Referring to last year's allegations of water tankers spraying water around air quality monitoring stations to bring down recorded pollution levels, Kharge claimed that this year PM2.5 readings had disappeared from 36 of Delhi's 59 monitoring stations as pollution peaked.He accused the Modi government of failing to address the problem despite identifying air pollution as a major challenge in 2019.Kharge cites pollution-linked deaths, unspent fundsThe Congress president also cited estimates of deaths linked to air pollution to underline the scale of the public health crisis.According to figures cited in his post, an estimated 17,188 deaths in Delhi in 2023 were attributable to particulate air pollution, accounting for nearly 15% of all deaths, based on Global Burden of Disease and Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air estimates.He also referred to the State of Global Air 2024 report, which estimated that 1,69,400 children under the age of five died from air-pollution-related causes across India in 2021.Kharge further questioned the utilisation of funds earmarked for tackling pollution in Delhi.Citing a September 2026 RTI response, he said Rs 1,154 crore, nearly 60% of Delhi's environmental compensation collections, remained unspent. He also claimed that the city had utilised only 17% of the National Clean Air Programme funds released up to December 2025.Kharge invokes Supreme Court deadline for statesKharge also pointed to the Supreme Court's direction to BJP-ruled Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan to submit detailed responses and proposed measures to tackle the pollution crisis within two weeks.He said the same pattern of toxic air, assurances and blame-shifting returned every year, particularly between October and February.“Year after year, particularly from October to February, the same toxic haze returns, accompanied by the same assurances and the same finger-pointing. Spend the funds. Cut emissions. articles.title: Cumbrian band behind star-studded Ukraine aid gig
articles.summary: Bob Geldof, Madness and Peter Hook are among acts billed for a concert in support of Ukraine.
articles.body:
A Cumbrian band who were the first British outfit to tour war-torn Ukraine is behind a star-studded gig in aid of women and children impacted by the conflict.

Hardwicke Circus have toured twice across music venues, hospitals and prosthetic centres in Ukraine since the war's outbreak.

They are behind Songs Of Freedom, a gig featuring Bob Geldof, Madness and Peter Hook, to be held at Manchester's Co-Op Live on 3 February and streamed worldwide.

Sir Paul McCartney, Barbra Streisand and Sean Penn will appear via video link at the event. It will be promoted by Harvey Goldsmith, who promoted Live Aid in 1985, organised by Geldof and Midge Ure to raise money for famine relief efforts in Ethiopia.

Hardwicke Circus' singer and guitarist Jonny Foster said it was "fantastic" to see so many big names support the idea, which the band came up with in the back of their tour van.

"I'm from Carlisle, I'm not in them circles whatsoever, but we were motivated by our tours of Ukraine."

Foster said the gig was less about the celebrity names and more about "music being a force for good".

"Music can play a powerful role in people's lives and it's a songwriters' night, showing support for Ukraine - music can offer that kind of positive influence and we're very lucky that everyone's come on board."

Goldsmith said he was "really pleased" to play a part in the fundraising event.

"We must stand together and play a role in pressuring the need to stop this war."

The Doobie Brothers, Chrissie Hynde, Nick Lowe, Inspiral Carpets, and Squeeze's Chris Difford will take to the stage alongside Ukrainian bands.

Foster said: "We saw the brutal destruction upfront [during our tours], we saw all the terrible things that are happening to their people, but we also saw a culture of joy and beauty and love and a desire to move forward into the future - it was that optimism of the Ukrainian people that we wanted to celebrate."

Money will be raised for charities United24, Voices of Children, Sviatoslav Vakarchuk Charitable Foundation (People Of The Future), and Masha Foundation.

Foster, whose band is rebranding to Jonny and the Hardwickes, explained the charities provided women and children with trauma support, de-mining and energy resilience for schools, among others.

Ahead of the concert, a special recording of the Ukrainian song Shchedryk (Carol Of The Bells) featuring the Songs For Ukraine Choir, the Royal Opera Choir and the London Metropolitan Orchestra will be released, also to raise money.

Foster said: "Through music we're going to show solidarity."

articles.title: Montreal man who rescued and nursed injured baby raccoon Pepper says he faces charges as he tries to stop wildlife authorities from taking her away
articles.summary: A Montreal man says he is facing an obstruction charge, along with a ticket authorities wanted to issue, after rescuing a baby raccoon named Pepper and
articles.body: A Montreal man says he is facing an obstruction charge, along with a ticket authorities wanted to issue, after rescuing a baby raccoon named Pepper and nursing her to health. Louka Berman found the seven-month-old animal at a construction site in May, where he said she and her mother had been shot with a crossbow. He intended to return Pepper to the wild, but attempts to release her have failed because she waits for him in the wooded area.After videos of the pair went viral, Quebec’s Environment Ministry sought the raccoon, accusing Berman of keeping her at home. According to Global News, Berman denies keeping Pepper at his residence and says he has hidden her in parks. He fears authorities may euthanise her and plans to challenge the charges in court.Montreal man rescues injured baby raccoon Pepper after crossbow attackLouka Berman found Pepper, a seven-month-old raccoon, injured at a construction site in May. He said, “Someone shot her with a crossbow, and they shot her too. So they thought that they were both dead.”He nursed her back to health. His intention, he said, was eventually to return the young animal to the wild. Pepper’s recovery, however, did not lead to a straightforward return to her natural habitat. Berman said she had become attached to him, and he described the bond as mutual.Berman struggles to release Pepper as she stays attached to himBerman said attempts to release Pepper into the wild had not succeeded. When he left her in a wooded area, she stayed and waited for him to return rather than moving away. He said Pepper had grown attached to him, and that he felt the same way about her. Videos showing Berman with Pepper later went viral, bringing wider attention to their relationship. Quebec’s Environment Ministry then came looking for the animal, accusing Berman of keeping her in his home. Authorities did not find Pepper. Berman insisted he was not keeping her at his residence and said he had instead been hiding her in parks. He said officials could come at any time to take her.Why is Montreal man Louka Berman facing charges over rescued raccoon PepperIn Quebec, a permit is required to keep a raccoon at home. Berman said he was not keeping Pepper at his residence, but authorities wanted to issue him a ticket over allegations that he was doing so. He said he was facing an obstruction charge. Berman planned to go to court to fight the charges. He said authorities could come at any time to take Pepper, and feared they might euthanise her.The Montreal SPCA’s Sophie Gaillard said the circumstances raised questions about whether Berman was legally in possession of the raccoon. She said, “It sounds like a situation where this animal would need to be rehomed in a wildlife sanctuary.”Why Pepper may need a wildlife sanctuary instead of returning to the wildGaillard said Pepper’s difficulty returning to the wild could indicate that the young raccoon had become habituated to people. She said the animal appeared to need a home in a wildlife sanctuary. Gaillard also pointed to a shortage of facilities in Quebec that can care for injured wildlife. The SPCA itself does not have the means to look after such animals and cannot always find another organisation that can take them in. She said, “Every year, we experience this issue where we have animals that, unfortunately, we have to euthanize because we can’t find a facility to take them in.”An online fundraiser has been launched in Pepper’s name to help fund a wildlife sanctuary. articles.title: Peter Pan mansion cafe forced to close after just over a year
articles.summary: The site at Moat Brae in Dumfries faced financial pressures and "ongoing difficulties behind the scenes".
articles.body:
A cafe and restaurant in part of the mansion which helped to inspire the Peter Pan story has shut after a little over a year.

Pan's Cafe opened at Moat Brae in Dumfries last summer about 12 months after the site had closed as a centre for children's literature.

However, owner Curtis Silver said increasing financial pressures, rising taxation and operating costs had led to the decision to shut being taken with a "heavy heart".

He added that "ongoing difficulties behind the scenes involving circumstances beyond our control" meant it was "impossible to continue in a sustainable way".

New owner outlines vision for Peter Pan mansion

Part of Peter Pan mansion to reopen as café

The property on the banks of the River Nith was where JM Barrie played as a child and he credited its gardens with helping to inspire his most famous work.

It was taken over by a trust and opened as a literature centre after a multi-million pound overhaul in 2019 but that project failed after five years and the property closed.

There were fears it could remain vacant - as it had for years previously - but the cafe reopened last summer alongside office spaces in the rest of the building.

However, despite a recent addition of its BRAE restaurant offering, the catering operation has not proved sustainable.

Silver said a combination of factors had made it "increasingly difficult to operate" and ultimately led to the closure.

"We're incredibly proud of what we've created, and even more grateful to everyone who has been part of it," he said.

"From our wonderful team who have worked so hard behind the scenes, to our loyal customers, familiar faces and everyone who supported us along the way thank you.

"We set out to create somewhere people could come together, enjoy good food and feel genuinely welcome.

"We hope that, in some small way, we achieved that."

He said the closure had come "sooner than we'd hoped" but they would "look back on the good moments with gratitude".

articles.title: Israeli forces kill Palestinian boy in West Bank, health ministry says
articles.summary: The Israeli military says its soldiers opened fire at individuals “who intended to hurl stones” at a road used by Israelis.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have shot dead a 14-year-old Palestinian boy during an operation in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say.

Moataz Daghlas was killed on Monday evening in the village of Burqa, north-west of Nablus, according to the Palestinian health ministry.

The Israeli military said soldiers identified "several terrorists who intended to hurl stones" in an area where stones had previously been thrown at Israeli vehicles. The soldiers fired towards them "to remove the threat", it added.

The Palestinian Red Crescent said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds, but that Israeli forces blocked their access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.

Moataz Daghlas's relatives said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.

Meanwhile, Palestinian news agency Wafa identified the two Palestinians wounded during the raid as a 17-year-old child, who it said was shot in the abdomen and pelvis, and a 19-year-old man, who was shot in the hand.

According to the UN, at least 98 Palestinians, including 22 children, have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year.

Six Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, it says.

The rules of engagement for Israeli forces were reportedly broadened after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, allowing soldiers increased discretion to use lethal force against a perceived threat.

In June, the UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory said it had verified the killing of 241 Palestinian children by Israeli security forces and settlers in the West Bank since then.

Most of the children were teenage boys and, in many cases, Israeli authorities accused them of having engaged in stone-throwing as justification, it found.

The UN office said its assessment was that none of the children killed while involved in confrontations with Israeli forces had posed an imminent threat to life, which it said was the only legal justification for the use of lethal force in the West Bank under international law.

articles.title: 'Our ties enjoy bipartisan support': India's first reaction to US midterm results
articles.summary: In its first reaction to the US midterm election results, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Tuesday chose to emphasise the bipartisan nature of
articles.body: In its first reaction to the US midterm election results, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Tuesday chose to emphasise the bipartisan nature of relations between the two countries while steering clear of commenting on the political outcome.The response comes against the backdrop of a significant political setback for US president Donald Trump, whose Republican Party lost control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.Democrats secured a sweeping victory, winning control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, in a result that is expected to constrain Trump's legislative agenda during the final two years of his presidency.Responding to a question on the midterm results, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the elections were an internal matter of the United States and declined to offer any specific assessment."It is an internal matter of the United States. I have no specific comment on them beyond underlining that India and the United States' relationship enjoys bipartisan support in the United States. We continue to work to further strengthen our comprehensive global strategic partnership that we share with the US," Jaiswal said.The MEA said New Delhi remained committed to strengthening its comprehensive global strategic partnership with Washington, signalling that it expects ties to remain a priority irrespective of which party gains political ground in the US Congress. For India, the outcome presents both opportunities and uncertainties.The two countries have witnessed considerable turbulence in their relationship under Trump's second presidency, with disagreements over trade tariffs, India's purchases of Russian oil, immigration restrictions and Washington's approach towards Pakistan emerging as major irritants.The Democratic takeover of Congress could provide New Delhi with additional avenues to engage with lawmakers who have traditionally supported stronger India-US cooperation. It could also increase scrutiny of the Trump administration's policies, including its approach to trade negotiations and foreign relations. However, a Democrat-controlled Congress does not necessarily translate into an immediate change in Washington's policy towards India.The US president retains considerable authority over foreign policy and trade negotiations, meaning Trump will continue to play a central role in determining the trajectory of bilateral relations. At the same time, congressional oversight could influence decisions involving defence cooperation, technology transfers, immigration and trade.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Amazon drone deliveries expand to 8,000 Darlington households
articles.summary: Amazon drones are now allowed to fly to 8,000 properties in Darlington, up from an initial 600.
articles.body:
Amazon's drone delivery service has been given permission to expand from 600 eligible households to 8,000.

The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has extended the licence for the service, known as Prime Air, to cover a wider area of Darlington where drones have been operating since May.

People with a garden, yard or driveway in the area served by the drones have been able to get deliveries in less than an hour on eligible items that weigh less than 5lb and can fit into a large shoebox.

Amazon said the new, higher level Sail 4 validation from the CAA, which allows drones to fly further and across urban areas, would mean more customers received items "quickly, safely and reliably".

Sophie O'Sullivan, from the CAA, said the extended authorisation "reflects the wider progress being made as the aviation sector evolves and new technologies become part of everyday operations".

Prime Air said its drones had machine-learning models to continuously monitor surroundings and recognise other aircraft, people, animals and physical obstacles that would not appear on a satellite map.

However, flights have not always been successful.

In July, the Air Accidents Investigation Branch launched a probe when a drone crashed into a Darlington garden.

No-one was injured, and Amazon claimed the drone "responded as designed".

articles.title: Republicans to pick new leaders after losing Congress: Scalise vs Jordan in House, Thune seeks to stay in Senate
articles.summary: As GOP faces criticism post-midterm elections, major leadership decisions are on the horizon in Congress with Scalise and Jordan competing for House minority leadership, while Thune aims to retain his Senate position. Discover how these changes will impact Republican strategy moving forward.
articles.body: Republican lawmakers in the US Congress are preparing to choose their next leaders as the party adjusts to losing control of both chambers following the midterm elections, with competing candidates emerging in the House and Senate.The leadership decisions, scheduled for Tuesday, will shape how Republicans approach their role in Congress when Democrats take over in January. The contests come amid growing criticism within the party over its election performance and its approach to President Donald Trump's agenda.In the Senate, John Thune is seeking to retain his position as Republican leader after the party moves into the minority. He appeared to face no challengers, although several conservative senators called for leadership voting to be postponed so lawmakers could first examine the reasons behind the election defeat.Thune said Republicans would discuss the results before proceeding with the vote.“I'm running for leader, but I think it's important that we have that discussion. And we will, and everyone will have a chance to weigh in, and then we'll hopefully move forward,” he told reporters on Monday.The House contest is more competitive, with Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan competing for the position of minority leader. Current Speaker Mike Johnson has ruled out seeking the post, leaving the two lawmakers to compete for the support of their Republican colleagues.Johnson, who struggled to maintain unity within the party during his tenure, predicted difficulties once Democrats assumed control of the chamber.“I'm sorry that voters made the wrong choice,” the Louisiana Republican said. “If we had kept the majority, we would stay on course.”The leadership elections will take place through secret ballots at the Capitol. Their outcome will determine who represents Republicans in both chambers during the final two years of Trump's presidency.Democrats secured at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate and 252 in the 435-member House, giving them control of both chambers ahead of the 2028 presidential election.Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party was preparing to advance its legislative priorities, including measures aimed at reducing living costs.“We're about to become the largest landslide in the history of the Senate since the '50s, and now we're ready to roll up our sleeves, get to work, and lower costs for the American people,” Schumer said on Monday.However, the incoming Democratic majority will still face limits on its ability to pass legislation. Most major bills in the Senate require 60 votes to overcome a filibuster, while overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers.Thune has pledged to work with Trump against Democratic proposals, particularly those aimed at reversing Republican policies on border security and judicial appointments. He has also faced criticism from Trump's supporters, who believe he did not push the president's agenda forcefully enough before the elections, including proposals for broader federal restrictions on voting.The leadership contest therefore comes as Republicans face two challenges: rebuilding their position after the election losses and deciding how closely their congressional strategy should remain aligned with Trump.You use AI every day.
